opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think one of the most interesting things we've seen is that bigger models don't just memorize more. They seem to actually compress the data better, and compression and generalization are really two sides of the same coin.

There's a nice intuition from the superposition work. A small model has very limited capacity, so it's forced to cram lots of features into the same neurons and directions. It ends up with these entangled, noisy representations, and it often falls back on shallow heuristics, like surface-level n-gram statistics, because that's the cheapest way to reduce loss. As you scale up, the model has room to represent more features more cleanly, and it can start learning circuits that capture the underlying structure rather than surface correlations.

You see this with things like grokking, too. Early in training, or in smaller models, you get memorization. But there's pressure, from weight decay or just from the sheer diversity of the data, that favors the more general solution, because one general circuit is cheaper than a thousand memorized special cases. Bigger models seem to find those general circuits more readily.

Another piece is sample efficiency. Larger models learn more from each example. If you show a big model a new concept a handful of times, it can slot it into this rich existing web of abstractions it already has. So the generalizations compound. Once you've got a good representation of, say, "deception" or "recursion," you can reuse it across code, stories, and math.

I'd add a caveat, though. Scale isn't magic. A lot of what we call "deeper generalization" is still fuzzy, and we don't have great tools to say whether a model is reasoning versus doing very sophisticated pattern matching. That's partly why I care so much about interpretability. If we can actually look at the features and circuits, we can stop arguing about it in the abstract and just check what's going on inside.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's complicated, and there are a few different things going on at once.

The simplest story is that bigger models have more capacity, so they can afford to learn more things. But that doesn't by itself tell you whether they learn deeper things or just more things. And actually, one of the surprising results from the interpretability work is that a lot of what a small model does is memorization dressed up as computation. If you look at what features it's learned, a lot of them are very specific, very brittle. They fire on this one token in this one context and that's it.

What seems to happen as you scale is that the model is under pressure to compress. It has to predict the next token across an enormous amount of data, and the parameters are a bottleneck relative to the data, even if the model is large. So the cheapest way to get the loss down is to find representations that are shared across lots of contexts. If you can have one feature that captures "this is a reference to a person who was mentioned earlier" rather than fifty features that each handle one specific name, that's a more efficient use of the weights. And that's exactly what a generalization is. So in some sense scale doesn't give you generalization for free, it gives you the incentive to generalize, because memorization stops paying off.

There's a nice way to see this with superposition. Small models are cramming way more features into their dimensions than they have room for, and a lot of those features are these very narrow, memorized things. Larger models, interestingly, seem to spend some of their extra capacity on more abstract features, things like "this code is going to throw an error" or "this is a statement about something the speaker is uncertain about." You don't really find those in tiny models. They just don't have the budget for them, and they don't need them to do okay on the training objective.

The thing I'd push back on a bit is the framing that it's a smooth continuum. From the outside, loss goes down smoothly with scale. But when you look inside, you sometimes see pretty discrete transitions, where a model goes from doing something by lookup table to doing it with an actual circuit. The grokking work is the toy version of that. And I think a lot of what we call emergence is just the aggregate of many of those little transitions happening at different scales for different capabilities.

So to directly answer the question: I think size matters a lot, but it's not that the model gets smarter in some uniform way. It's that at each scale there's a different set of things where the general solution becomes cheaper than the memorized one, and the model finds it. And then the interesting question is whether the general solutions it finds are the same ones we would have found, or whether they're these alien, efficient compressions that happen to work. And my guess is it's a lot more of the latter than people would like.

astra-6.text:
I think scale helps, but I’d distinguish getting more things right from forming a deeper generalization. A larger model can get better by remembering more patterns, without necessarily discovering a principle that unifies them.

But those two things aren’t mutually exclusive. If you’re trying to predict language across lots of different contexts, there’s an incentive to discover reusable structure. Instead of learning a thousand separate associations, you might learn one abstraction that explains all of them. A larger model has more capacity to represent those abstractions and the intermediate steps needed to use them.

The tricky part is figuring out which of those explanations accounts for an improvement. I’d want to see what happens when you change the surface details or combine familiar concepts in an unfamiliar way. Does the model still apply the underlying principle? That’s much stronger evidence of a deeper generalization than just a higher score on examples that look like its training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scale helps because it gives the model room to represent the structure behind the examples, rather than just learning a collection of surface-level associations. If lots of different observations can be explained by the same underlying rule, learning that rule is a very efficient way to predict the data.

But I wouldn’t equate a larger model with a deeper understanding automatically. A larger model also has more capacity to memorize. What matters is the interaction between capacity, the diversity of the training data, and the pressure training puts on the model to find reusable structure.

The interesting test is whether a model can take something it learned in one context and use it in a genuinely different one. Does it still work when you change the superficial details? That’s much stronger evidence of a deeper generalization than just getting more familiar questions right.
